title: Tesla’s Cybercab Officially Launches Today. It’s Already Under Investigation
author: Aarian Marshall
text: Tesla’s Cybercab, a distinctive two-seater without a steering wheel or brake pedals, is set to start picking up members of the public in Austin, Texas, this evening. But the vehicle is already under investigation by the US federal government, which is probing whether it meets federal safety standards.The investigation comes just hours after the electric automaker welcomed hundreds of fans to downtown Austin to ride in the driverless Cybercabs. Tesla plans to deploy the vehicles on its Robotaxi ride-hail network, which is currently operating in a handful of cities in Texas and Florida.The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration is updating vehicle standards to make it easier and faster for driverless cars to deploy on public roads. It’s currently tweaking eight rules, including those requiring car parts that driverless cars don’t really need: brake pedals, windshield wipers, and rearview mirrors. But for now, years-old standards remain in place.Featured VideoThis Guy Made Two Bots Talk to Each Other Because He Was So Fed Up With AI InterviewsMeanwhile, unusually shaped robotaxi companies have been told to apply for an exemption from federal rules before they start picking up passengers. Amazon subsidiary Zoox, whose vehicles do not have steering wheels or manual controls, won the first of these exemptions this summer, which limits its operations to 2,500 vehicles this year.Tesla, however, has said it doesn’t need an exemption because its vehicles comply with all existing safety standards.The investigation, called an Audit Query, will examine the data and process that Tesla used to make that determination, according to a government filing.In a statement, NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison said his agency “fully supports the safe development and deployment of automated vehicles. But as the federal regulator, we need to ensure that all of our laws are followed.”Tesla did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Ann Carlson, a former acting NHTSA administrator who is now a professor of environmental law at UCLA, says the investigation is likely “an indication that NHTSA is super frustrated with Tesla.” The agency made clear through the Zoox case that it expects driverless vehicle developers to go through the exemption process. “For Tesla to slap them in the face and ignore that—that is gobsmacking,” she says.This kind of federal investigation can prove consequential. NHTSA can require an automaker to change its vehicle or process. The agency can also pursue enforcement actions, including civil penalties. Volvo Group North America paid $130 million in penalties in 2023 after an investigation into its recall process. The company also agreed to three years of oversight by a third-party auditor.The Cybercabs are, in many ways, symbols of Tesla’s intended future. CEO Elon Musk has said that Tesla should no longer be regarded as an automaker, but as a robotics and autonomous vehicle company. While 45 of these vehicles are in Texas’ Tesla fleet right now, a state database shows, the company intends to deploy millions annually.Updated at 3:55 pm ET on September 4: We've added comments from acting NHTSA administrator Ann Carlson.Most PopularGearTesla’s Make-or-Break Cybercab Had a Quiet DebutBy Aarian MarshallGearAI Use in the Job Market Is Creating an Infinite Doom LoopBy Jill DuffyGearCasio’s Leaked G-Shock ‘CasioNaut’ Looks a Lot Like a Patek Philippe ClassicBy Jeremy WhiteComputersWe Just Got Our First Real Look at AI PCs With Nvidia’s RTX Spark ‘Superchip’By Luke Larsen
